title: William Ames: without predetermination man would be God's partner, not his subject
source_text: XLI. Ejusmodi causarum secundarum praemotionem & praedeterminationem, ac praecipue humanae voluntatis, admittendam statuit Gul. Amesius; quia alioquin, ipsius judicio, tolletur subordinatio causae primae & causarum secundarum in suis operationibus. Subtrahentur dominio providentiae, & gubernationi Dei efficaci, operationes omnes Voluntatis humanae. Homo non subditus, sed socius Dei erit. Imo Deus pendebit ex hominis nutu, etiam in iis quae praecipuam rationem habent in totius mundi procuratione. Nec homo dicere debebit, Si Deus voluerit faciam hoc aut illud; sed potius Deus dicere debebit, Si homo voluerit faciam hoc aut illud. In Bellarmino Enervato tomo quarto, libro quarto, capite secundo.
pass_a_gloss: Such premotion and predetermination of second causes, and chiefly of the human will, Will. Ames lays down is to be admitted; because otherwise, in his judgment, the subordination of the first cause and of second causes in their operations will be taken away. All operations of the human Will will be withdrawn from the dominion of providence, and from the efficacious government of God. Man will be not a subject, but a partner of God. Nay God will depend on the nod of man, even in those things which have the chief account in the administration of the whole world. Nor will man have to say, If God will I shall do this or that; but rather God will have to say, If man will I shall do this or that. In Bellarmine Enervated tome four, book four, chapter two.
pass_b_english: William Ames holds that premotion and predetermination of this kind must be admitted for secondary causes, and above all for the human will. Otherwise, in his judgment, the subordination of secondary causes to the first cause in their operations would be done away with.

Every operation of the human will would be removed from the rule of providence and from God's efficacious government. Man would be God's partner rather than his subject. Indeed God would hang on man's nod even in matters that weigh most in governing the whole world. Man would no longer have to say, 'If God wills, I shall do this or that'; rather God would have to say, 'If man wills, I shall do this or that' (Bellarminus enervatus, tome 4, book 4, chapter 2).

lemmas.latin: Homo non subditus, sed socius Dei erit
lemmas.gloss: Man will be not a subject, but a partner of God

choices.why: Kept as the Thomist technical term; Le Blanc explains 'physical' as opposed to 'moral', not to 'supernatural'.
